pll1d2c5-d1e3476.summary: Transition to the New Testament, using the images of the two animals (Hab 3:2) and the coal taken from the altar (Isa 6:6) for the Testaments jointly revealing the truth that touches the mouths of the faithful.

pll1d2c5-d1e3497.summary: Interprets Christ's baptismal command with Ambrose: 'in the name,' not 'names,' shows unity of essence, and the three names declare three persons.
claims: 'In the name' (singular) shows the unity of essence.
The three names show three persons.

pll1d2c5-d1e3535.summary: Reads John 10:30 with Ambrose: 'one' rules out any division of power or nature, and 'are' distinguishes Father and Son, so the perfect Father begot a perfect Son, one by unity of nature, not by confusion.
claims: 'One' excludes difference of power or nature.
Father and Son are one by unity of nature, not confusion.

pll1d2c5-d1e3576.summary: Cites 1 John 5:7: three bear witness in heaven, Father, Word, and Spirit, and these three are one.
claims: The three heavenly witnesses are one.

pll1d2c5-d1e3596.summary: Reads John 1:1 as showing that the Son was always and eternally with the Father, as one person with another.
claims: The Word was eternally with the Father as distinct from him.

pll1d2c5-d1e3608.summary: Cites Gal 4:6, 'He sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts,' as Paul's clear distinction of the Trinity.
claims: Paul distinguishes Father, Son, and Spirit.

pll1d2c5-d1e3622.summary: Adds Rom 8:11 on the Spirit of him who raised Jesus dwelling in us, as a further Pauline indication of the three.

pll1d2c5-d1e3634.summary: Interprets Rom 11:36 with Augustine: 'from him' refers to the Father, 'through him' to the Son, 'in him' to the Spirit. The singular forms, not 'from them' or 'to them glory,' show the Trinity is one Lord God.
claims: 'From', 'through', and 'in him' correspond to Father, Son, and Spirit.
The singular pronoun shows the three are one God.

pll1d2c5-d1e3677.summary: Concludes the scriptural dossier: since almost every syllable of the New Testament attests unity and Trinity, Lombard stops gathering testimonies and turns to show by reasons and fitting likenesses, as far as weakness allows, that it is so.
claims: Nearly all of the New Testament attests the unity and Trinity.
The doctrine will next be shown by reasons and similitudes.

pl-l1d2c5.summary: Moves to New Testament testimonies to the unity and Trinity: the baptismal formula 'in the name' (singular, one essence) of three persons; 'I and the Father are one' (unum against division, sumus against confusion); the three witnesses (1 Jn 5:7); John 1:1; Paul's Trinitarian formulas; and Romans 11:36, where ex, per, in correspond to Father, Son, and Spirit, but the singular ipso/ipsi shows one God. Since nearly every syllable of the New Testament attests this, Lombard ends the citations and turns to reasons and similitudes.
claims: The baptismal formula shows one essence ('in the name') and three persons (three names).
'I and the Father are one' excludes both division of nature and confusion of persons.
Romans 11:36 signifies the three persons and, by its singular, one God.
The New Testament everywhere attests the unity and Trinity.
After authorities, reasons and similitudes are to be given.
